idiom_name: opaque struct + add/at/count functions over a hand-managed array
implementation_notes: C has no collection machinery to lean on: the collection is a struct with a pointer, a length and a capacity, and the invariant-owning API is a set of functions compiled beside it. Keep the struct definition in the .c file and publish only an incomplete type plus constructor/destructor and named operations (orders_new, orders_add, orders_at, orders_count), so callers cannot touch the buffer or the length directly - GLib's GPtrArray makes the opposite choice and exposes pdata and len as public fields, which is exactly the leak the pattern exists to prevent. Return elements as const pointers and never as a writable array; if callers need to traverse, provide orders_foreach with a callback, or a pointer plus count pair that the documentation marks read-only. Ownership must be part of the contract: whether add copies the element or takes over the pointer, and who frees elements on clear and on free.
pitfalls: Handing out the struct definition or the internal array lets any caller write past len or bypass orders_add; keep the type incomplete in the header.
A capacity-growing realloc moves the buffer, so element pointers returned earlier dangle; document that accessor pointers live only until the next mutation.
Ownership is unwritten by default: without an explicit destructor and ownership contract the collection leaks or double-frees elements on clear and free.
Macro-based 'generic' collections lose the type and bounds checks exactly where the invariant should be enforced; keep type-specific functions so the compiler objects to misuse.
